title: Digi Yatra International Trials Start November 1 at Seven Airports
excerpt: Indian nationals with e-passports flying Air India or IndiGo can test face-based entry, security and boarding — immigration and document checks stay unchanged.
body:
• Digi Yatra international trials go live on 1 November 2026 and run through December at seven airports: Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai, Cochin and Amritsar.
  • Eligibility is narrow: Indian nationals holding an e-passport, flying internationally on Air India (all destinations) or IndiGo (select destinations).
  • To enrol, create an e-passport credential in the Digi Yatra app before travel — scan the passport's machine-readable zone, tap the chip with an NFC phone, take a selfie — and keep the credential in the app wallet.
  • Carry your passport as usual: airline document checks and immigration are unchanged in this trial, and Digi Yatra works only at enabled entry, security and boarding points.

Digi Yatra, the facial-recognition system that lets domestic passengers move through Indian airports without repeatedly showing documents, is about to be tested on international departures. The Digi Yatra Foundation has begun the beta phase of its International Passenger Trials at seven airports, with the trials scheduled to go live on 1 November 2026 and run through December, according to the announcement reported by Travel Trade Journal.

Who can use it, and where

The trial airports are Delhi, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Cochin, Mumbai, Chennai and Amritsar. Eligibility is limited to Indian nationals holding e-passports who are travelling on international flights operated by Air India or IndiGo. The trial covers all international destinations served by Air India and select destinations operated by IndiGo, as Travel Trends Today reported. Eligible passengers can use Digi Yatra at terminal entry, the Security Hold Area and boarding gates, subject to infrastructure availability at each airport.

That eligibility list is the detail diaspora travellers should read first. An Indian citizen with a newer e-passport flying Air India from Delhi to the United States is inside the trial. A foreign passport holder, an OCI cardholder travelling on a foreign passport, or a passenger on another airline is not, on the terms announced. Neither is an Indian national whose passport predates e-passports and has no embedded chip.

How enrolment works

The international credential is built from the passport, not from Aadhaar as in the domestic system. In the Digi Yatra app, the passenger scans the passport's Machine Readable Zone, reads the embedded chip using a compatible smartphone's NFC capability, captures a selfie and verifies the details. The result is an e-passport-based Verifiable Credential stored in the passenger's Digi Yatra wallet on their own device, consistent with Digi Yatra's decentralised, self-sovereign identity design, as described by Media Infoline.

Doing this at home, before the travel day, is the practical move. NFC chip reading can fail on a first attempt depending on phone and passport placement, and an airport queue is the wrong place to discover that. Passengers must still carry their travel documents and complete mandatory airline document checks, immigration procedures and other formalities as usual. The trial speeds up the airport's own checkpoints. It does not replace the border.

Why the Foundation is moving carefully

Digi Yatra Foundation chief executive Suresh Khadakbhavi said the international trials extend a model that has already changed domestic travel, and pointed to interoperability with global frameworks such as IATA's One ID and ICAO's Public Key Directory as part of the path ahead, "helping explore how e-passport-based digital credentials can enable more seamless and secure passenger journeys across borders, while keeping passenger consent, privacy and security central to the experience."

The domestic base is large. Digi Yatra now reports more than 26.5 million users and over 110 million journeys facilitated, across 39 domestic airports and 11 domestic airlines, with average airport adoption of about 30%. The app is available in 11 regional languages, with expansion to all 22 scheduled languages by 2027, and another 25 domestic airports are planned by 2027. Alongside the trial, the Foundation has released a redesigned app with a cleaner interface, airline-coloured boarding-pass displays and a clearer consent screen explaining what information is shared, with whom and for what purpose.

What to watch

The December end date makes this a test, not a rollout. The questions that will decide what follows are operational: how many eligible passengers complete the credential step, how reliably the gates read e-passport credentials at seven different airports, and whether entry and security times fall without document-check queues simply moving to boarding. For now, eligible Air India and IndiGo passengers departing from the seven airports from 1 November have a faster lane to try, provided they enrol before they leave home and keep the passport in hand.
